name: Crimean Gothic
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Attested only via Busbecq's 16th-c. wordlist; no stress description possible or located

new_statements.quote: Auch die nebentonigen Silben haben nach dem Ausweise des y von treithyen an der Tonlängung teilgenommen. Wie im Deutschen ist auch im Krimgot. die Tonlängung eine Folge der besonders starken exspiratorischen Betonung des Germanischen. (p. 169) Die Vokale der unbetonten Silben sind durchweg zu Überkürzen, die etwa die Qualität eines a hatten, geschwächt worden. (p. 170) So ist vielleicht möglich, dass in zwei ursprünglich viersilbigen Wörtern mit hochbetonter Anfangssilbe und drei folgenden kurzen Silben, in wichtgata aus *hwita-gata und malthata aus *mali-deda, dasselbe Synkopierungsgesetz zur Tilgung der zweiten Silbe geführt hat (p. 171)
new_statements.translation: The secondarily stressed syllables too, as the y of treithyen shows, took part in the lengthening under stress. As in German, lengthening under stress in Crimean Gothic is a consequence of the especially strong expiratory accent of Germanic. (p. 169) The vowels of unstressed syllables have throughout been weakened to overshort vowels of roughly the quality of an a. (p. 170) So it is perhaps possible that in two originally four-syllable words with a strongly stressed initial syllable and three following short syllables, wichtgata from *hwita-gata and malthata from *mali-deda, the same syncope law led to the deletion of the second syllable (p. 171)
new_statements.citation: Loewe, Richard. 1896. Die Reste der Germanen am Schwarzen Meere. Eine ethnologische Untersuchung. Halle: Max Niemeyer.
new_statements.locator: pp. 169, 170, 171 (chapter 'Die Sprache der Krimgoten', pp. 136-177; PDF pages 189-191 of the saved text-layer PDF, printed page = PDF page - 20)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Loewe treats Crimean Gothic as carrying the inherited Germanic strong expiratory stress on the root = initial syllable ('hochbetonte Anfangssilbe'), with the second member of compounds/compound numerals (treithyen '30') carrying secondary stress; unstressed (non-initial) vowels are reduced to overshort schwa-like vowels or syncopated. This is an analyst's assumption applied to Busbecq's 1562 word list, not a statement derived from any accent marking in the data.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress ('nebentonige Silben') on the second element of compound numerals, e.g. treith-yen '30' (p. 169); proclitics/enclitics (ich, tzo, the/tho) said to be still more weakly stressed than unstressed syllables of full words (pp. 137, 168 n., 172).
new_statements.exceptions: None as exceptions; Loewe notes the material is too scanty to set up definite syncope/apocope laws (p. 171) and that thiin-ita shows elision before a following 'hochbetontem langem Vokal' (p. 171).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated citation forms in Busbecq's Latin-glossed list plus a 3-line song). The corpus (c. 80 words, 1562) has no accent marks, so any stress statement for Crimean Gothic is reconstructive; Loewe's 'Betonung' passages presuppose Germanic initial stress rather than demonstrate it.
new_statements.identity_note: Crimean Gothic (crim1255) is known almost entirely from Busbecq's 1562 letter (printed 1589): about 80 words and a 3-line song written down by a Flemish speaker from a Greek-speaking informant, with no accent marks; ninth/tenth-century Mangup graffiti (Vinogradov & Korobov 2015-2018) add nothing on prosody. Loewe 1896 analyses exactly this corpus, so no dialect issue arises, but every stress claim is a reconstruction based on Germanic initial stress plus vowel-reduction patterns in the spellings.

sources.note: Vowels treated under 'Vokale der betonten Silben' vs 'der unbetonten Silben' (pp. 136-137); p. 169: stressed short vowels lengthened, a consequence of 'der besonders starken exspiratorischen Betonung des Germanischen', secondary-stressed syllables (treithyen '30') also lengthened; p. 170: unstressed vowels weakened to overshort a-like vowels, liquids/nasals take over the syllable accent; p. 171: wichtgata, malthata treated as four-syllable words 'mit hochbetonter Anfangssilbe' -> Germanic root-initial stress assumed throughout, never argued from the data (Busbecq gives no accent marks).
Lists only Stearns 1978 and Stearns 1989 (subclassification comments); no descriptive references.

'The etymologically inconsistent spelling of vowels in unaccented syllables probably indicates vowel reduction, likely to schwa' -- second-hand, no placement rule; its bibliography (Stearns 1978/1989, Grønvik 1983, Nielsen 2017, Miller 2019, Peters 2020, Vinogradov & Korobov 2018) used for discovery.

sources.citation: Fulk, R. D. 2018. A Comparative Grammar of the Early Germanic Languages. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (Studies in Germanic Linguistics 3), open access, §1.13.
sources.note: One paragraph on Crimean Gothic (Busbecq 1562/1589, c. 80 words + song; Cercignani's caveat against lineal descent from Bible Gothic; refers to Stearns 1989, Grønvik 1983); nothing on its stress. The book's accent chapter treats Proto-Germanic initial stress generally, not Crimean Gothic.
